transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-07-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Li, Jordan Kim (Redwood)  Rajiv Patel, Emily Wong, Marcus Lee, Olivia Chen (Cascade)
Notes: deep technical session focused on KV cache eviction, paging, prefix-reuse across long-context workloads and VPC/private deployment considerations

Summary (auto):
- Investigated root causes for cache thrashing observed in Cascade's production traces; likely interplay of aggressive KV cache eviction + prefix reuse behavior + bursty user sessions with long contexts.
- Discussed paging (KV sharding to host memory / SSD), eviction heuristics (LRU vs TTL vs frequency-aware), and batching implications.
- Action: Redwood to provide design doc + bench harness; Cascade to provide token distribution and sample sessions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samantha Li: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is sam from Redwood, i'll kick us off  want to make sure we cover the eviction traces you sent and then demo some knobs we can tune, sound good?
[00:07] Rajiv Patel: yeah thanks, appreciate it. we saw a lot of generation hiccups around, uh, 10 to 20k token sessions where responses slow down and occasionally we hit 503s.
[00:14] Jordan Kim: thanks for the context. quick clarifying q: those 503s  are they coming from our gateway timeout or backend timeouts?
[00:19] Emily Wong: looks like backend, sorry network is messy, but stack traces show the runtime evicting large KV pages and then repeatedly refilling them, so tail latency spikes.
[00:30] Jordan Kim: mm-hmm, that matches a few patterns. two suspects: one, your seq length distribution has high variance so the KV cache exceeds per-GPU memory, and two, prefix reuse is low and evicted keys are immediately needed again (thrashing).
[00:45] Marcus Lee: can you define prefix reuse quickly? we call it "context reuse" internally  users sending similar prefixes but not exact matches.
[00:51] Priya Rao: sure  prefix reuse here means identical token prefixes that let us reuse KV cache entries; if prefixes differ slightly (like variable user ids injected) you lose reuse.
[01:00] Rajiv Patel: yeah our chat templates include per-session personalization tokens which vary, so we suspected prefix reuse is low. but some customers have identical system prompts so reuse should exist.
[01:09] Jordan Kim: perfect. so two levers: heuristics for grouping/pinning prefixes, and smarter eviction that considers anticipated reuse probability rather than pure recency.
[01:20] Samantha Li: we'll go through the runtime knobs  Jordan, can you pull up the eviction slide? (brief pause) 
[01:27] Jordan Kim: yep  slide shows eviction strategies: LRU, LFU (frequency), TTL, and proactive pinning plus soft-reservations for hot prefixes. in practice we combine frequency with recency and a small adaptive TTL to avoid oscillation.
[01:42] Emily Wong: does that require additional bookkeeping that impacts token-time? we saw CPU spikes on our control plane when we tried heavier metrics.
[01:49] Jordan Kim: good point  there's overhead. our implementation keeps per-prefix counters with exponential decay (cheap) and a compact bloom-like hot set to avoid scanning full tables. CPU cost is small relative to saving repeated KV recompute for large prefixes.
[02:03] Marcus Lee: what about paging to host memory or NVMe? we have constrained GPU RAM and can't just increase memory.
[02:09] Priya Rao: yes, paging is an option  we support a tiered KV store: GPU DRAM hot set, host RAM warm set, and NVMe cold pages. degree of asynchronous prefetching matters; naive paging adds latency.
[02:23] Rajiv Patel: in our traces, the runtime did page and performance collapsed because prefetch wasn't aligned with access pattern  we got a synchronous page fault.
[02:33] Jordan Kim: exactly. two approaches: synchronous fallback (simple but slow) vs async prefetch heuristics driven by lookahead of token windows. for chat workloads we can often predict next prefixes and prefetch those KV shards.
[02:45] Samantha Li: can we share an example? Marcus, you have that trace with repeated token jumps, right?
[02:50] Marcus Lee: yep I'll paste it  (short pause, someone shares link) the pattern shows users open big threads then jump to a different branch, causing large KV churn.
[03:01] Jordan Kim: that's classic branching-induced eviction. a practical mitigation is per-session pinning: keep recent prefixes for active sessions pinned for a short window to avoid losing them on a branch switch. that uses more RAM but reduces refill.
[03:14] Emily Wong: how do you decide pin duration? too long and we blow memory; too short and thrash continues.
[03:20] Jordan Kim: adaptive  pin duration is a function of observed session activity and reuse probability score. we favor shorter pins for low-reuse sessions. default pin is 30s, but you can tune per-tenant.
[03:30] Rajiv Patel: is tenant-level tuning available in private/VPC deploy? we need control without code changes.
[03:35] Priya Rao: yes  with Redwood Private we expose config flags in the control plane UI and API; you can set per-customer pin budgets and eviction policy profile.
[03:44] Olivia Chen: what about quantization effects on KV size? we're running 4-bit for cost reasons.
[03:49] Jordan Kim: quant reduces KV footprint but some quant formats require dequant/requant steps that affect refill time. 8-bit quant tends to have better tradeoff for KV because the memory drop is moderate but compute overhead smaller.
[04:01] Marcus Lee: hmm we saw slightly higher tail latency with 4-bit during refill, likely due to extra ops.
[04:07] Jordan Kim: that aligns  we can recommend mixed precision: the KV store kept in 8-bit and attention weights in 4-bit, or compress KV with a fast lightweight codec.
[04:18] Rajiv Patel: are there any recommended kernel changes? our infra team asked about optimized memcpy for NVMe->GPU for paging.
[04:25] Priya Rao: our runtime leverages batched pinned transfers and unified memory where available; optimizing IO path is critical. we avoid small random reads by organizing KV shards contiguously per prefix group.
[04:36] Emily Wong: could we batch evictions to reduce overhead? right now evictions happen per-token in our setup.
[04:42] Jordan Kim: batching evictions helps  we maintain a soft threshold and perform tidy-up rounds that evict less-favored keys in micro-batches, which amortizes overhead. downside is transient oversubscription but usually controlled.
[04:55] Marcus Lee: ok that's helpful. can you talk about prefix normalization strategies? we suspect small differences in user ids are killing reuse.
[05:01] Samantha Li: yes normalization is low-hanging fruit  strip deterministic per-user identifiers from prefixes, replace with placeholders, or hash variable segments so identical logical prompts map to same prefix key.
[05:12] Rajiv Patel: will that break personalization? some prompts need the id for context.
[05:16] Jordan Kim: it's a tradeoff we recommend placeholdering non-critical tokens and keeping a short local context window with per-session state for user-specific data. that retains personalization while enabling prefix reuse for the bulk of the prompt.
[05:29] Olivia Chen: are there tools to help us identify parts to normalize?
[05:32] Samantha Li: we can run a prefix similarity analyzer on your logs  produce a report showing opportunities for placeholdering. Jordan can add that to the bench script.
[05:39] Jordan Kim: yep adding it to action items.
[05:42] [06:00] (fast-forwarded notes)
[06:00] Jordan Kim: i want to highlight the importance of lookahead and batching at the runtime layer. if we can collect tokens in small groups and predict next prefix windows, prefetch becomes effective.
[06:11] Marcus Lee: how does batching interact with latency SLO? our product needs 200ms p95.
[06:16] Jordan Kim: continuous batching is tuned by max wait and max batch size. for strict latency SLOs you lower max wait and accept smaller batches; Redwood's runtime optimizes micro-batches (~4-8 tokens) with low overhead to maintain p95.
[06:29] Priya Rao: also consider hybrid routing: route latency-sensitive users to dedicated capacity (reserved GPUs) with larger pin budgets.
[06:35] Rajiv Patel: that might be ok  we have top-tier customers who need consistent p95. what's cost tradeoff?
[06:40] Samantha Li: Dedicated ups cost but gives predictable latency; Redwood Optimize can estimate cost delta for your observed token distribution  we'll run that in follow-up.
[06:48] Emily Wong: back to eviction heuristics  any cases where TTL alone works?
[06:52] Jordan Kim: TTL is simplest for workloads with predictable session lengths; for bursty or branching sessions TTL alone can be too blunt. combination heuristics tend to work best.
[07:02] Olivia Chen: you mentioned frequency counters with decay  can you share expected memory overhead?
[07:07] Jordan Kim: a compact 8-bit decayed counter per prefix plus a 64-bit key fingerprint  roughly 16 bytes per tracked prefix; so 1M prefixes ~16MB, plus hash table overhead. manageable compared to KV values.
[07:20] Marcus Lee: our observed hotset is about 200k prefixes  that seems feasible.
[07:25] Jordan Kim: yeah that's small.
[07:28] Rajiv Patel: what about cross-GPU sharing? our model shards across two GPUs and KV is split  sometimes a prefix exists on GPU0 but request lands on GPU1.
[07:36] Priya Rao: we do local-first then peer fetch; peer fetching can be costly. in Dedicated setups we co-locate session affinity so a session sticks to same shard when possible; otherwise we replicate tiny hot entries across GPUs. replication vs fetch is a tradeoff.
[07:50] Jordan Kim: replication of a tiny hotset reduces latency but increases memory; peer fetch maintains lower memory but has jitter. affinity scheduler often wins for chat-type sessions.
[07:59] Emily Wong: about logs  we want better observability to spot eviction-caused refills; current metrics are coarse.
[08:05] Samantha Li: Redwood Console exposes per-prefix eviction counters, refill latency histograms, and per-tenant hotset sizes  we can grant Cascade a trial dashboard for this.
[08:14] Rajiv Patel: please do. also we need audit logs for Private deploys.
[08:17] Priya Rao: audit logs and KMS integrations are supported  we'll send the security doc (next steps).
[08:23] Marcus Lee: there's a weird pattern we saw where prefix reuse is high but eviction still occurs  could this be hashing collisions?
[08:29] Jordan Kim: possible if fingerprinting is tiny. we use 64-bit fingerprints to minimize collision; collisions at that size are extremely unlikely. more likely is key canonicalization mismatch or invisible whitespace.
[08:40] Olivia Chen: newline vs space differences, yep.
[08:44] Jordan Kim: normalization step should fix that.
[08:47] Rajiv Patel: can you outline a bench plan for us? we want to reproduce the tail latency locally.
[08:52] Jordan Kim: plan is: 1) ingest your token distribution and session traces; 2) run baseline on courtesy-hosted infra (small cluster) to reproduce eviction + refill; 3) run controlled experiments toggling pin budgets, quant settings, and eviction policy; 4) produce a matrix of p50/p95/p99 and cost. we'll need the logs and a sample dataset.
[09:11] Samantha Li: and Jordan will add prefix-sim report and bench harness link.
[09:16] Emily Wong: what about NVMe throughput? our disks are SATA in a few edge sites.
[09:21] Priya Rao: NVMe is strongly recommended for paging; SATA will cause high latency. we can provide a hybrid plan: keep hotset on GPU+host RAM and avoid paging on SATA sites, or we can recommend upgrading to NVMe for heavy long-context workloads.
[09:35] Rajiv Patel: what's the recommended GPU memory per active concurrent session? rough rule of thumb?
[09:40] Jordan Kim: depends on model and average seq length. rough: for a 70B model with 8k context, plan ~20-28GB of KV per active session if not quantized aggressively; with 8-bit quant and optimized KV layout you can reduce 2-3x. we'll provide model-specific guidance.
[09:57] Marcus Lee: that's a wide range  we'll share exact model and avg tokens.
[10:00] Samantha Li: other questions from Cascade?
[10:03] Olivia Chen: are there any quick mitigations we can toggle in production this week?
[10:06] Jordan Kim: yes  three quick low-risk changes: 1) enable prefix normalization for templates, 2) increase pin budget for high-tier sessions by small percent, 3) switch KV storage to 8-bit if currently 4-bit for KV only. all low-friction and reversible.
[10:20] Rajiv Patel: can you implement 1) and 2) via config?
[10:24] Priya Rao: yes we can flip config flags in your Private control plane; for hosted we'll need to schedule a config rollout but it's still quick.
[10:33] Emily Wong: how long to see improvement after config flips?
[10:36] Jordan Kim: often within minutes to hours depending on session churn; the bench will prove it.
[10:42] Samantha Li: ok, quick recap and next steps  we'll share: 1) KV cache design doc and eviction heuristics (Jordan), 2) bench harness + prefix-sim tool (Jordan), 3) security and Private deployment docs (Priya), 4) Redwood Console dashboard trial (Samantha). Cascade will share session traces and token distributions. schedule follow-up benchmark week of 2027-07-26.
[10:59] Rajiv Patel: sounds good, appreciate the time.
[11:02] Marcus Lee: thanks all.
[11:05] Samantha Li: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links. bye.

End of call.
